claims.text: Replacing a standard EAM reference with a machine-learned interatomic potential will improve reference–target phase-space overlap during thermodynamic integration of high-temperature high-entropy alloys.
The proposed method applies to multicomponent high-entropy alloys in both solid and liquid states near melting.
The ML potential should be trained on ab initio data covering diverse local atomic configurations found in the liquid.
The approach is applicable to alloys containing five or more principal elements.
The applicable temperature range is approximately 0.85–1.05 times the melting temperature.
Liquid configurations are especially diverse in the stated near-melting temperature range.
The ML potential captures many-body and local-environment effects that EAM misses.
Capturing these effects bridges the configurational gap between the ab initio target and the reference system.
Training on a broad set of ab initio configurations allows the ML potential to represent the liquid-state energetic landscape better than traditional EAM potentials.
The ML potential represents liquid-state structural variability better than traditional EAM potentials.
Better representation of the energetic landscape and structural variability improves overlap between configurations sampled by the reference and ab initio target systems.
Improved reference–target phase-space overlap reduces thermodynamic-integration path mismatch.
The ML reference is expected to reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch by approximately 30–50% relative to TOR-TILD EAM references.
The reduced path mismatch will yield free-energy estimates that more closely reproduce ab initio target values.
TOR-TILD calculations currently use EAM reference potentials.
The method may be less effective when the training dataset omits rare or extreme configurations.
The method may be less effective when important electronic-structure effects fall outside the training-data domain.
Performance may vary outside high-temperature regimes.
A comparative study using the same representative alloy near melting can test ML and EAM references against an ab initio target.
Failure to achieve a statistically significant reduction of at least 30% in path mismatch, or failure to improve free-energy convergence toward the ab initio benchmark, would falsify the hypothesis.
